The ratio comes from first-step entropy reduction under a fixed Ibis0 classifier: 0.155 versus 0.062 bits. Holding the evaluator fixed makes comparisons consistent, but entropy reduction can reward confident errors and is not itself evidence of improved prediction of the true label. It also favors selection strategies compatible with that evaluator’s beliefs. The label-aware trajectory in Figure 5 is helpful, but the reported reduction in experiments is 30–40% relative to random, with only a slight improvement over prompted Opus 5. These are different claims. Evaluation should include sequential Brier/log loss, experiments required to reach a prespecified predictive target, alternative belief evaluators, and computational cost. Using frontier models within the same EIG procedure would also help separate the benefit of calibration from that of the selection algorithm.

The benchmark split remains problematic, although the filtering analysis is reassuring.
Appendix A.7 reports that test-target measurements appear in training or validation evidence for 0.6% of Tahoe, 10.1% of DepMap, and 53.2% of GWAS episodes. The filtered evaluation shows small aggregate changes and unchanged rankings, so this does not justify dismissing the main forecasting result. Nevertheless, an intended benchmark should prevent this overlap by construction. A rebuilt split should also be used for the simulator and experiment-selection experiments. Entity-, study-, or locus-held-out evaluations would better establish generalization beyond interpolation within the source resources.

The belief-update calibration metric has important interpretive limitations.
Appendix C acknowledges that stochastic probability outputs attenuate the estimated slope toward zero, potentially exaggerating “overreaction.” It also excludes zero updates, which account for up to 68% of updates for Ibis0 non-thinking, and conditions on starting belief using only five bins. These choices complicate comparisons across models with different output granularity and noise. Moreover, marginal calibration alone does not guarantee the claimed update-calibration identity; a stronger conditional calibration assumption is needed. Repeated probability estimates, sensitivity to stratification, and validation against a known calibrated Bayesian predictor would make the conclusions more convincing.

The practical calibration comparison and scientific scope need more careful framing.
Appendix H shows that a two-parameter recalibration substantially closes the zero-shot forecasting gap. The dismissal of this approach because it requires labels is unconvincing when Ibis0 itself uses extensive labeled training data. A comparison using a fixed validation set and matched label budgets would be more informative. Also, probabilities systematically below the empirical support rate demonstrate underprediction of support, which is not necessarily “underconfidence” in the conventional sense. Finally, the labels represent whether a particular assay satisfies a threshold, rather than whether a biological proposition is ultimately true. The balanced sampling and structured evidence format should remain central to the interpretation.

Questions for the authors

Can the main forecasting and experiment-selection results be reproduced on splits that exclude all test-target measurements from training evidence and simulator training?

What assumptions justify treating marginal Bayes-factor additivity as a coherence requirement for the mirrored evidence pairs?

Does the EIG advantage persist under sequential proper scoring rules and alternative belief evaluators, including when frontier models use the same EIG selection procedure?

Summary

AO-Flow addresses single-image 3D generation using generated orbit videos. Its first contribution is a cross-stage conditioning interface: sparse-structure generation reads all 49 frames and retains regional source identities and attention masses, which Shape generation subsequently uses as priors while recomputing content attention. The receiver is trained sequentially, freezing the sparse-structure producer before adapting Shape. Its second contribution is asset-oriented video post-training: the receiver is frozen, and video attention LoRA is optimized using final-asset geometry, hidden-surface coverage, and input-preservation rewards.

The reported results show improved hidden-region reconstruction over global four-view conditioning and further improvements from asset feedback. The regional interface offers a favorable receiver quality–cost trade-off relative to dense reading, while video post-training trades some input fidelity for better completion.

Strengths

Well-motivated cross-stage interface. Retaining regional source identities while allowing Shape to recompute attention is a sensible way to reuse coarse-stage information without forcing the refinement stage to inherit the same final attention distribution. Capturing memory from the actual sampling trajectory also avoids an additional selection probe.

Useful controlled receiver comparisons. Table 2 includes global selection, dense reading, Shape-selected routing, uniform source priors, removal of spatial bias, and independently trained Shape-no-video conditioning. Region-4 achieves H-F 0.639 versus 0.613 for Global-4 at nearly identical receiver cost. Relative to Full-49, it reduces receiver time from 166.2 to 98.2 seconds and peak memory from 47.8 to 32.0 GB, with a modest H-F reduction from 0.645.

The evaluation acknowledges competing objectives. The authors report input preservation, failures, and an independent structural checklist rather than relying exclusively on the optimized surface metrics. They explicitly acknowledge that Asset-DPO is competitive and that asset RL worsens input-view agreement. Inference uses a single unselected sample.

Detailed implementation specification. The appendices carefully distinguish reference information used for supervision/reward from inference inputs, actual sampled memory from GT support, and stochastic training from deployment sampling. The discussion correctly acknowledges that clipping is inactive under the single-update policy schedule.

Weaknesses

Uncertainty is missing for the comparisons most relevant to the contribution. Appendix H states that the main tables use one training replica and one deployment draw per object. The three-replica/four-draw evaluation and bootstrap intervals are described as a full-run plan, but their results are not presented. This is particularly consequential for Region-4 versus Shape-selected-4 (0.639 versus 0.635), mass-matched regional versus global routing (0.631 versus 0.625), and Asset Flow-GRPO versus Asset-DPO (0.669 versus 0.667). The structural difference between the latter methods is only two passing objects out of 100. These results need paired uncertainty estimates and, for the central small differences, training-seed variation.

The evidence supports the complete interface more strongly than its proposed mechanism. The regional/global H-F gap falls from 0.026 to 0.006 under the retained-mass control. This suggests that changes in real/null allocation account for a substantial part of the original comparison. The paper recognizes this confound and specifies useful support-aware global selection, region–source reassignment, and local-cue interventions, but does not report their outcomes in the PDF. Likewise, sequential producer freezing is motivated but not directly compared with an alternative training schedule. Consequently, the evidence for specifically transferring useful regional information across stages remains incomplete.

The added value of online Flow-GRPO is limited by the reported trade-off. Asset-DPO achieves nearly the same H-F with better input IoU (0.910 versus 0.906), better LPIPS (0.160 versus 0.169), and lower reported post-training cost (790 versus 864 GPU-hours). This supports final-asset feedback as a useful objective, but provides weaker evidence for preferring the online optimization procedure. Geometry-video RL also uses less compute and better preserves the input. A comparison at matched compute and comparable preservation would clarify the practical benefit.

Compute accounting needs reconciliation. Appendix G.2 states that Asset-DPO and Best-of-4 SFT use the same saved initializer pool of 1,000 records and four videos/assets per record. However, Table 13 assigns them substantially different candidate-generation costs (420 versus 220 GPU-hours) and scoring costs (250 versus 80). Different fitting costs are expected, but the discrepancy for the shared pool requires explanation. Additionally, the PDF specifies substantial S1/S2 work, including potentially 80,000 SS memory rollouts, without reporting corresponding total training durations. End-to-end inference latency including video generation is also needed to contextualize the receiver-only speedup.

Several claims are backed by protocols rather than reported measurements. The appendices describe reward-ranking audits, controlled defects, local evidence interventions, sampler-transfer evaluation, and annotation agreement, but do not provide their numerical outcomes. The structural pass rates are useful, yet agreement statistics and component-level results would make them more assessable. The manuscript should clearly separate completed experiments from proposed diagnostics.

Generalization evidence remains narrow. GSO transfer is encouraging, but its inputs are protocol renders rather than real photographs. The principal qualitative system comparison contains three character examples, and the reported corruption table covers only one blur condition. Broader qualitative coverage and real-image examples would help assess robustness to the nominal-camera assumptions and the mismatch between GT-orbit receiver training and generated-video inference.

Questions for the authors

Can you provide paired confidence intervals and replica-level results for the regional/global, regional/Shape-selected, and Flow-GRPO/DPO comparisons?
Which of the specified mechanism and reward-audit experiments have actually been completed? What are their results?
How should Table 12’s common 0.72/0.28 mass figures be interpreted relative to the per-region downward matching rule and the separate posterior-partition diagnostic?
Why do shared-pool generation and scoring costs differ between Asset-DPO and Best-of-4 SFT?
Does Flow-GRPO retain an advantage at comparable input preservation and compute, and how sensitive are its gains to downstream receiver randomness?

Overall assessment

The regional receiver is a promising contribution with a useful reported efficiency trade-off. Asset-oriented feedback also appears beneficial. However, the evidence currently falls short of establishing the smaller mechanism-specific gains and the advantage of online RL, while incomplete diagnostic reporting and unresolved cost accounting weaken the overall case. Repeated-run results, completed mechanism tests, and reconciled cost measurements could materially improve my assessment.

Suggested rating: 5/10 — marginally below the acceptance threshold.
Confidence: 3/5 — moderate; based on detailed manuscript inspection, without code or supplementary-package verification.

Summary

The paper proposes k-Support Pruning (KSP), a post-training method for N:M LLM sparsity. It regularizes layerwise reconstruction error with blockwise squared k-support norms, derives a weighted proximal operator, and obtains executable masks through hardening followed by a masked conjugate-gradient refit. The theoretical analysis establishes per-block convex-hull tightness, a conditional certificate for lossless hardening, and support recovery under diagonal curvature. Extending the norm to fractional budgets yields a resource-allocation objective whose marginal costs are squared water levels. Experiments compare uniform pruning and mixed allocations across multiple model families and scales, including latency-matched evaluations at 70B.

Strengths

A coherent and useful formulation. The connection between N:M constraints and blockwise k-support regularization provides a principled alternative to fixed rankings and nonconvex support search. The weighted proximal operator makes the formulation computationally actionable, and the relationship to activation-scaled saliency helps explain existing methods within the framework.

Substantial empirical coverage. The evaluation spans several model families, multiple sparsity patterns, perplexity and downstream accuracy, and models up to 70B. KSP is competitive with strong reconstruction-based baselines, including ALPS. The authors also examine calibration changes, allocation transfer, quantization, and recovery fine-tuning.

Useful controls on compensation and allocation. Giving different masks the same refit is a valuable experiment. Table 11 shows that much of the gap to ranking-based methods comes from compensation, while some differences between masks remain. Running ALPS under KSP’s allocation is similarly informative and avoids attributing every improvement to the selector.

Attention to actual hardware costs. The latency-matched comparisons are more convincing than parameter-count comparisons alone. In Table 15, latency-priced allocation improves WikiText-2 perplexity from 4.610 to 3.716 at the same reported 1.078× prefill speedup. The simple “free-dense” control also provides a useful deployment lesson.

Weaknesses

The scope of “tight relaxation” is narrower than parts of the presentation suggest. Proposition 1 concerns the convex hull of an N-sparse, norm-bounded set. It does not establish that the penalized reconstruction objective in Eq. (3) is an exact relaxation of the original unconstrained-scale N:M reconstruction problem, or that hardening its optimum gives an optimal support for general dense Grams. Indeed, the unbounded cardinality-constrained set itself has a trivial convex hull. Appendix B appropriately qualifies the aggregation as a modeling choice, but the main text repeatedly uses broader language about a relaxation “tight for the constraint.” The distinction between tightness of the block gauge and tightness of the pruning optimization should be explicit.

There is also a concrete overstatement in §3.3: the claim that the relaxed optimum, hardened mask, and refitted solution “all” coincide with the combinatorial optimum is inaccurate. Even under diagonal curvature, the relaxed weights generally retain shrinkage for

λ>0; Proposition 2 establishes support recovery and optimality after refitting.

The practical relevance of the certificate is insufficiently demonstrated. Corollary 1 characterizes when the proximal output already has integral gates, making hardening leave that block unchanged. This is useful, but conditional, and does not certify combinatorial optimality under dense curvature. I did not find measurements of the fraction of certified blocks, how this fraction changes along continuation, or the actual reconstruction-loss increase from hardening uncertified blocks. These diagnostics would connect a prominently advertised theoretical contribution to the reported models. Finite-iteration ADMM results should also distinguish certification of the proximal variable from convergence to the convex optimum.

The allocation price is exact for the surrogate, but its relationship to final quality remains empirical. Equation (9) minimizes the regularizer’s value at fixed weights. Its derivative is therefore an exact marginal price for that objective, not automatically the marginal improvement in reconstruction after pruning and refitting, or in downstream accuracy. The paper acknowledges “in the penalty,” but broader statements about directly pricing the value of sparsity sometimes obscure this limitation. Comparisons with random allocation and OWL are useful; a reconstruction-based allocator under the same measured-latency budget would be a stronger test. The substantial free-dense improvement also arises without the proposed water-level allocator and should remain clearly separated from its contribution.

Compute and statistical controls limit some empirical conclusions. Table 4 reports 2,200 seconds for the main KSP configuration versus 1,570 seconds for ALPS on 3B. The reduced and reported KSP configurations change both solver and computational budget, so their difference does not isolate preconditioning or search quality at fixed cost. Quality-versus-time curves would make the comparison stronger. Some headline accuracy wins are also very small—for example, 42.49 versus 42.47 on 1B and 52.03 versus 51.98 on Llama-2-7B—and should be interpreted with uncertainty estimates. The 75% sparsity experiments and central 3B comparison use single runs.

More generally, Figure 3 compares effects measured from different starting configurations and, for allocation, different densities. These are informative individual contrasts, but do not establish a universal ordering of the four decisions.

Novelty and reproducibility need sharper delineation. The paper cites the relevant k-support and box-norm literature, but should identify precisely which results are new extensions. McDonald, Pontil, and Stamos already develop the variational box-norm framework and efficient proximal computation for its square. The pruning application, weighted formulation, and allocation integration should be distinguished from that established machinery.

The PDF also defers important configuration details—continuation settings, stopping rules, and baseline commands—to released code. Explicit pseudocode for the reported ADMM solver and a compact configuration table would make the submission more self-contained. Hardware results would benefit from fuller timing protocols and decode measurements in addition to prefill.

Questions for the authors

What fraction of blocks satisfies the hardening certificate in the reported configurations? How much does hardening change reconstruction loss before refitting?
At matched wall-clock budgets, how do KSP and ALPS compare? Does the advantage persist when both receive identical final masked-CG compensation?
Which weights and normalization constants are used to compute allocation scores? How well do these scores predict measured reconstruction improvements after refitting?
How does water-level allocation compare with a reconstruction-based allocation baseline at matched latency?
Are the 70B speedups measured end to end or aggregated from component timings? What precision, batch size, sequence length, and offloading configuration are used?

Rating justification

I lean toward acceptance because the formulation is useful, the implementation appears practical, and the experiments contain meaningful controls beyond standard benchmark comparisons. However, I view this primarily as a strong methodological integration and empirical contribution. Stronger claims of optimal support selection or exact pricing of downstream quality are not established.

Soundness: 3/4 — generally solid, with important qualifications needed.
Presentation: 3/4 — organized, but some central claims are overstated.
Contribution: 3/4 — useful synthesis with substantial evaluation.
Confidence: 3/5 — moderate; based on the manuscript and selected prior literature, without code inspection or reproduction.

My assessment is borderline, leaning reject: the reusable selection framework is useful and the experiments are promising, but the paper needs stronger evidence that its modest gains are reliable and specifically attributable to model adaptation. Summary

The paper proposes MARS, a framework for task-specific instruction-data selection that separates reusable candidate characterization from model-specific calibration. An external LLM annotates candidate examples along six ability dimensions. For each target task and base model, response-NLL percentile ranks on a small reference set determine ability-level selection quotas and difficulty-weighted reference profiles. Candidates are then selected through within-bucket profile matching. This avoids recomputing model-dependent features over the candidate pool when changing base models.

Experiments use a 270,699-example pool, four pretrained model families, five target tasks, and a 5% selection budget. MARS achieves the highest average performance among the compared selection methods on each model, with approximately 1.0–1.3-point improvements over the strongest baseline, while substantially reducing repeated selection computation.

Strengths

Clear and practically relevant problem formulation. Separating reusable candidate representations from lightweight model-specific feedback is a sensible approach when selecting data for multiple models. The computational advantage follows directly from the design: new models require evaluation only on the reference set.

Consistent results across model families. Table 1 shows improvements in average performance on all four models, rather than a benefit confined to one backbone. The comparison includes several technically different selection methods, random selection, and full-data training.

Substantial supporting analysis. The paper includes component ablations, calibration ablations across all four models, bidirectional MARS subset transfer, alternative NLL weighting schemes, a second annotator, and ability-decomposition experiments. In particular, Table 10 provides a more direct test of recipient-specific calibration than comparisons against transferred subsets from other methods.

Generally clear presentation and useful implementation details. The annotation prompt, quota rounding, tie handling, missing-profile fallback, and API token accounting are documented. These details make the method easier to understand and potentially reproduce.

Weaknesses

The reliability of the performance gains is not established. No multi-seed results or uncertainty estimates are reported. This matters because the improvements over the strongest baselines are approximately one point on average, and some individual differences are very small. MBPP contains only 500 evaluation examples, while BBH uses 40 examples per subtask. The reported consistency is encouraging, but training-seed variation and paired evaluation uncertainty are needed to assess whether the ranking is robust. Likewise, the calibration improvement for Gemma is only 0.68 points on average.

Robustness to the reference set is a central unresolved issue. The method derives both quotas and reference profiles from as few as nine examples for TyDiQA, with one example per language. NLL ranks may reflect language, tokenization, or response-format differences as well as the intended ability deficits. Percentile normalization removes absolute scale differences but does not resolve these within-set confounds. The paper should vary reference-set size and composition and report the stability of allocations, selected subsets, and downstream performance. The weighting-scheme ablation in Appendix C.1 does not address this sampling sensitivity.

The comparisons do not fully isolate the value of the proposed ability representation. The existing ablations establish that components help within MARS, but do not show whether six manually defined abilities outperform simpler reusable representations. Particularly useful controls would be quality-only selection, reusable embedding-based matching, and coarse task/domain buckets with the same NLL-based calibration. The ability-distribution-matching baseline removes both quotas and calibration, so it changes several components simultaneously. The related-work discussion acknowledges skill-based allocation, but the empirical distinction from simpler forms of that approach remains incomplete.

The connection between ability allocation and selected-data composition needs validation. Equation 2 computes a soft ability distribution, but selection converts it into quotas over hard dominant-ability buckets. Consequently, selecting a fraction

A complete comparison should include annotation latency, all major baselines, and amortization across different numbers of models.

The experimental scope limits the broader data-efficiency claim. All results use one candidate pool and one selection budget. Two epochs over the full pool also entail substantially more optimization steps than two epochs over a 5% subset, so outperforming full-data training does not isolate selection quality from training-duration effects. Additionally, MARS remains below the untuned Qwen base model on average and loses five points on GSM8K. This does not invalidate the selection-method comparison, but warrants a clearer discussion of when targeted SFT helps versus merely reduces degradation.

Questions for the authors

Do the main improvements persist across training seeds and independently sampled reference sets, especially for TyDiQA?
How does MARS compare with quality-only selection and reusable embedding or coarse-domain representations under the same calibration procedure?
What fraction of selected examples changes across models? Can you report subset overlap, achieved ability composition, and the frequency of missing-profile or quota-overflow fallbacks?
What is the end-to-end selection time including annotation, and how does the cost–performance comparison change when including MoNA?
How were design choices selected without using test performance, and can you release exact reference/evaluation IDs, annotations, and baseline configurations?

Overall assessment

The paper presents a useful engineering contribution with encouraging empirical breadth. My main reservations concern statistical reliability, reference-set sensitivity, and whether the proposed ability framework adds value beyond simpler reusable alternatives. The existing appendix experiments address several obvious concerns, but do not resolve these central questions. Positive results on repeated runs and stronger reusable baselines would materially improve my assessment.

Suggested rating: 5/10 — marginally below the acceptance threshold.
Confidence: 3/5 — reasonably confident in the assessment, with code-level reproduction and independent verification of related work outstanding.

My assessment is borderline reject: the approach is plausible and the appendix provides useful supporting evidence, but the evaluation does not yet establish the necessity of the proposed components or robust generalization. This review is based on the full manuscript, including its appendices.

Summary

The paper studies prediction of spot-level cell-type abundance from H&E images. It combines a ResNet18, GATv2, and Transformer backbone with two training objectives. KGSC identifies potentially confusable cell-type pairs using LLM-generated biological descriptions, PubMedBERT embeddings, and training-set abundance correlations, then supervises their standardized relative abundances. RSGC supervises spatial abundance differences using enrichment- and gradient-dependent weights. Experiments on Human Lung, HER2ST, and STNet show improvements over the evaluated baselines.

Strengths

Relevant problem and coherent motivation. Distinguishing related cell types and preserving spatial abundance transitions are meaningful challenges. Matching observed spatial differences, rather than simply encouraging neighboring predictions to agree, is a sensible design.

Consistent aggregate improvements. The method achieves the highest mean PCC and SCC among the evaluated methods across all three datasets. Table 1 reports three-seed results, and Table 2 suggests that both auxiliary objectives contribute.

Useful supporting analyses. The appendix goes beyond selected visualizations: Table 5 compares structured semantics against raw evidence; Table 7 examines the selected confusion pairs; Table 4 evaluates spatial gradients; and Figure 5 assesses inter-cell-type spatial associations. These analyses provide some evidence consistent with the intended mechanisms.

No additional semantic input at inference. Biological descriptors and auxiliary supervision are used during training, while inference requires image patches and spatial adjacency.

Weaknesses

The evaluation does not establish generalization to unseen patients. Section 4.1 specifies tissue-section-level splitting, but multiple sections come from the same donors or patients. Section separation prevents shared spots, but does not necessarily prevent donor-specific morphology or technical effects from appearing in both training and testing. The manuscript should report exact train/validation/test assignments and whether donors overlap. Patient-disjoint evaluation is particularly important for Human Lung, which contains only four donors. This is an unresolved protocol issue, rather than evidence that leakage occurred.

The gains are modest, and their robustness is insufficiently characterized. Relative to Hist2Cell, the absolute PCC improvements in Table 1 are 0.011, 0.009, and 0.011 on Lung, HER2ST, and STNet, respectively. These may be useful, but three training seeds do not capture uncertainty across patients or data partitions. Most ablations use a single seed, as disclosed in Appendix A.4. Paired section- or patient-level results and repeated patient-disjoint splits would make the evidence more convincing. The seed variation alone does not establish whether the gains are statistically reliable.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed mechanisms sufficiently. Table 5 is a useful comparison, but it does not establish whether semantic pair selection is better than correlation-only selection, lineage-based selection, or random pairs matched in number and coverage. Similarly, RSGC should be compared with an unweighted gradient-matching objective and variants removing enrichment weighting, gradient weighting, and center normalization. Without these controls, the improvements could arise primarily from adding pairwise and spatial auxiliary supervision, rather than from the proposed knowledge and reliability mechanisms. Comparisons with CUCA and HP-Cell, both discussed as direct prediction methods, are also absent.

“Reliability” is inferred from magnitude rather than demonstrated. Equation 44 assigns larger weights to larger target gradients. This is a reasonable importance heuristic, but a larger difference is not necessarily a more reliable measurement. The evaluation uses Cell2location-derived reference abundances, which are inferred targets rather than direct cell counts. Large differences could also reflect deconvolution error. Robustness across alternative deconvolution targets, uncertainty-aware weighting, or controlled target perturbations would help substantiate the reliability claim.

The interpretation of KGSC requires greater precision. KGSC constrains differences between cell-type-specific standardized abundances. Consequently, the sign of its target difference describes relative enrichment compared with each type’s training distribution; it does not generally describe which cell type has greater absolute abundance at a spot. Claims about correcting “abundance ordering” should make this distinction explicit. In addition, Table 7 reports baseline ordering error for selected pairs but omits ordering error after KGSC, despite this being a direct measure of the claimed correction. Its significance tests also need their test procedure and sampling unit specified, accounting for dependencies among pairs that share cell types.

Spatial improvements are not fully established for the deployed output. Table 4 provides encouraging improvements in gradient direction accuracy, from 0.4767 to 0.5781, and gradient Spearman correlation, from −0.0423 to 0.1572. However, gradient MAE changes only from 0.7483 to 0.7460, and these results concern the local branch rather than the final averaged prediction. The spatial association and selected JSD analyses are helpful, but final-output gradient and boundary metrics across all three datasets would more directly support the central spatial-recovery claim. Absolute abundance errors should also accompany PCC and SCC, which do not establish calibration.

Important semantic-learning details remain unspecified. Appendix A.1 describes a residual projection, Transformer, and reliability-aware common/specific field selection, but does not adequately specify the semantic representation learning objective or training procedure. Since these embeddings determine the confusion graph, this omission affects reproducibility. The complete descriptors, exact generation prompt and settings, semantic encoder implementation, and resulting pair sets should be provided.

Questions for the authors

Are the splits patient/donor-disjoint? Please provide exact assignments, the validation protocol, and checkpoint-selection criteria.
How much improvement remains with correlation-only or matched random pair selection, and with unweighted spatial gradient matching?
What objective trains the semantic projection, Transformer, and common/specific aggregation components?
Does KGSC reduce the selected pairs’ ordering error, and do RSGC’s gradient improvements persist in the final prediction across datasets?
How are the abundance targets constructed and normalized, and how sensitive are the conclusions to the deconvolution method?

Presentation

The main method is reasonably organized, and the appendix documents many implementation constants. However, the distinction between inferred reference targets and biological ground truth should be clearer. Figure 6 uses independently scaled abundance maps, which limits visual assessment of magnitude accuracy; shared scales would improve comparison. The manuscript should also clarify how Table 1 aggregates correlations across sections and cell types, and distinguish within-dataset evaluation on multiple datasets from cross-dataset transfer.

Overall assessment

The paper presents a promising application of biologically informed pairwise supervision and spatial gradient matching. However, the current evidence leaves uncertainty about patient-level generalization, the added value of the specialized weighting mechanisms, and the reproducibility of semantic representation learning. These are central to assessing the contribution, so I currently lean toward rejection. Patient-disjoint results and targeted controls demonstrating benefits over simpler auxiliary objectives would materially strengthen the case.

Suggested ratings: Soundness: 2/4; Presentation: 3/4; Contribution: 2/4.
Recommendation: Borderline reject.
Confidence: 3/5 — the assessment follows the manuscript and appendix; implementation correctness and experimental reproducibility have not been independently verified.

My assessment is weak reject, with promising empirical results but insufficient evidence that reaching equilibrium is the source of the main gains. This review incorporates the appendices; I have not run the supplementary code.

Summary

The paper formulates fixed-length text generation as a game in which token positions are players and tokens are actions. When the full-context conditionals derive from a common joint distribution, unilateral best-response updates increase sequence probability, and pure Nash equilibria correspond to coordinate-wise local maxima. The authors propose selecting the position with the largest conditional-probability improvement and prove an approximate-equilibrium convergence bound. Experiments apply this procedure to pretrained masked language models, demonstrating improved QA performance over one-shot masked generation and several autoregressive baselines, alongside smaller gains over confidence-ordered masked generation.

Strengths

Clear formulation and correct core argument. The potential-game interpretation provides an intuitive characterization of token-level stability. Theorem 1’s multiplicative-improvement argument appears correct under its stated compatibility and positive-initial-probability assumptions. The exponential separation construction is also straightforward and valid.

Interesting use of frozen masked models for generation. Obtaining useful zero-shot QA outputs from relatively small encoder models without additional training is noteworthy. For example, Ettin-400M achieves 61.79 F1 on the filtered CoQA subset and 72.76 on the full development set. The full-set evaluation usefully addresses concerns about the answer-length filter.

Useful controlled comparison and extensive diagnostics. The ModernBERT-chat comparison holds the backbone fixed, making it more informative about decoding than cross-model comparisons. The appendices provide confidence intervals, timing measurements, initialization ablations, representative failures, and lexical-overlap statistics.

Transparent reporting of limitations. The authors explicitly acknowledge incompatible masked-model conditionals, report cycles, and measure violations of pseudo-likelihood monotonicity. These disclosures strengthen the empirical analysis.

Weaknesses

The algorithmic novelty needs clearer positioning against coordinate ascent and iterated conditional modes. Under compatible conditionals, the proposed update is discrete coordinate ascent on joint log-probability; its equilibrium is a coordinate-wise local optimum. Sequential maximization of local conditionals is the central idea of iterated conditional modes (Besag, 1986). The paper should explain precisely what is new beyond the game-theoretic interpretation, maximum-gap scheduling, and application to language generation. The current related-work discussion omits this particularly close connection.

Moreover, the convergence argument does not fundamentally require selecting the maximum-gap coordinate: any update with conditional-probability improvement exceeding ε yields the same multiplicative lower bound. Maximum-gap selection may be useful empirically, but its specific benefit is not established by this proof.

The theoretical guarantees do not cover the main experimental method. Theorem 1 assumes conditionals compatible with a common joint distribution and ε > 0. The main experiments use potentially incompatible masked-model conditionals and ε = 0, with additional stopping rules. Appendix C reports cycles in 6/500 WikiText trajectories and pseudo-likelihood increases on only 75.2% of updates. These are appropriately acknowledged, but they substantially limit the connection between the theorem and the implemented decoder.

Consequently, the main-text language about monotonic likelihood improvement and polynomial-time decoding needs tighter qualification. The result bounds token replacements in terms of log(1/p₀) and 1/ε under a conditional-query model; it is not an unconditional polynomial-runtime guarantee for the experimental implementation. Likewise, Figure 2’s running-minimum diagnostic does not demonstrate monotone convergence of the actual gap or validate the theorem for masked models.

The experiments do not sufficiently isolate the value of equilibrium-seeking revision. One-shot prediction of every masked position is a weak baseline for iterative masked generation. Much of the improvement over it could arise from sequentially supplying context, rather than revisiting tokens or reaching equilibrium.

The same-backbone comparison in Table 3 is helpful, but the improvements over confidence ordering are modest: approximately +1.23 F1 on CoQA, +0.37 on PubMedQA, and +0.32 on CLAPNQ. Appendix H reports that the CLAPNQ confidence interval includes zero. These gains require approximately 6.6×, 33×, and 48× as many model calls, respectively.

Appendix G.1 further reports that revisions constitute only 2.5–4.4% of updates and that answer quality largely saturates before exact convergence. This suggests that construction order may explain much of the benefit. Comparisons against confidence-ordered construction on the untuned backbones, followed by controlled revision schedules and early stopping, are needed to establish the central contribution.

The evaluation protocol limits the broader generation claims. Every method receives a reference-derived output length, and EOS is banned. Although consistently applied, this is an oracle setting. The masked model additionally observes the remaining answer slots directly, while the autoregressive model does not receive an equivalent representation of the target length. Thus, identical length constraints do not necessarily provide equivalent information.

The benchmarks also emphasize lexical overlap: Appendix D reports that 99.1% of CoQA answer tokens and 97.6% of CLAPNQ answer tokens occur in the context. This does not invalidate the results, and PubMedQA provides a useful counterpoint, but F1/ROUGE alone offer limited evidence about factual correctness and general generation quality. Predicted-length evaluation, natural stopping, and a groundedness or correctness assessment would strengthen the claims.

Parameter-count comparisons overstate the practical advantage. The “18× larger” comparison is accurate for selected baselines but does not control for inference compute, training data, or model quality. Appendix H reports approximately 10.5 and 17.4 seconds per question for ModernBERT Nash decoding on PubMedQA and the timed CLAPNQ subset, versus 0.8 and 1.1 seconds for Falcon. The work would be more compelling with quality-versus-compute curves and stronger decoding baselines at comparable budgets.

Questions for the authors

How much improvement remains when confidence-ordered construction, max-gap construction without revisions, and full Nash decoding are compared on each untuned masked backbone?

Starting from the same completed sequence, how do maximum-gap, cyclic, and random-coordinate revision compare at matched compute? Does maximum-gap scheduling materially improve quality or convergence cost?

What happens when the answer length is predicted without reference access? How sensitive are the results to modest overestimation or underestimation?

Can you report equilibrium, cycle, and update-cap termination rates for every backbone and dataset, including ModernBERT-chat, together with quality at several positive ε thresholds?

What contribution is intended beyond iterated conditional modes, and can the abstract and main-text claims explicitly distinguish exact-joint guarantees from masked-model empirical behavior?

Minor comments

The introduction uses log-probability utilities, whereas additive ε-equilibrium is defined using probability differences. Exact best responses coincide, but approximate equilibria depend on this choice; the distinction should be explicit.
Equation 2 should use membership in the argmax set to accommodate ties.
Appendix H should report a finite-resolution bound rather than a permutation-test p-value of exactly zero.
Appendix G.1’s statement that six CoQA examples are the “only non-converged trajectories in our experiments” should be reconciled with the six WikiText cycles in Appendix C.

Overall assessment

The paper offers a useful perspective and an interesting empirical demonstration of generation with frozen masked models. However, the novelty relative to established local optimization is underdeveloped, the guarantees do not apply to the main implementation, and the experiments do not yet establish that equilibrium-seeking provides enough benefit over simpler iterative decoding to justify its cost.

Suggested rating: 4/10 — weak reject.
Confidence: 4/5. The main mathematical argument and experimental limitations are clear; implementation fidelity remains unverified.

My provisional assessment is weak accept: the paper makes a substantial empirical and systems contribution, although some claims about modality, compression, and generality exceed what the experiments establish. This review is based on the supplied manuscript and appendix; I have not independently verified novelty against external literature.

Summary

This paper introduces PixelRAG, a retrieval-augmented QA system that indexes rendered webpage screenshots and provides retrieved image tiles directly to a vision-language reader. The system scales to approximately 30 million tiles from 7.1 million Wikipedia articles, with an additional news corpus. It adapts a pretrained single-vector visual embedding model using synthetic queries, contrastive learning, and filtered hard negatives. The paper evaluates text-centric QA, multimodal QA, and agentic search, and explores reader fine-tuning for lower-resolution screenshots.

The main contribution is a convincing demonstration that screenshot-based retrieval can operate at a substantial corpus scale and improve downstream QA, including on questions that do not intrinsically require images. The algorithmic components are relatively conventional; the contribution lies primarily in their integration, scale, and empirical investigation.

Strengths

Substantial scale and practical relevance. Operating over the full English Wikipedia corpus is a meaningful step beyond small document collections. The single-vector design makes the index comparatively manageable, and the paper provides concrete rendering, storage, and latency measurements.

Consistent improvements across several settings. In Table 1, PixelRAG improves over Trafilatura from 55.9% to 58.7% on NQ, 42.5% to 48.8% on NQ-Tables, and 71.6% to 78.8% on SimpleQA. The base visual retriever also improves over the text baselines, indicating that the benefits are not solely attributable to additional training. The news results provide useful evidence beyond Wikipedia.

More extensive baseline coverage than the main table alone suggests. The appendix includes learned extractors, full-corpus sparse–dense hybrid retrieval, matched text-retriever training, HTML-based alternatives, and a small-scale ColPali comparison. These controls materially strengthen the paper. The reported paired significance test on NQ-Tables is also helpful.

Useful investigation of where improvements arise. The retrieval–reader modality ablation distinguishes benefits of visual retrieval from benefits of visual reading. The evidence-level analysis and examples of lost tables and displaced paragraphs provide plausible explanations for the gains. The discussion of fixed tiling and split tables is particularly informative.

Weaknesses

The strongest text controls are not evaluated end to end. Tables 11 and 12 report article-level Recall@1 for hybrid retrieval and matched-trained text retrieval, while the main conclusions concern QA accuracy with three retrieved items. These results establish a retrieval advantage under those configurations, but do not quantify the final QA gap against the strongest text pipeline. In particular, matched training and hybrid retrieval are evaluated separately. Reporting QA accuracy and evidence Recall@3 for their combination would make the central comparison substantially stronger.

The modality ablation does not fully isolate preservation of webpage structure. “Text → Rendered image” renders already-extracted text, so it cannot recover structure or content lost during extraction. “Screenshot → OCR” is informative, but introduces OCR errors and changes the representation simultaneously. The observed SimpleQA difference between screenshot reading and OCR reading is only 1.6 percentage points in Table 3, without uncertainty estimates. Thus, the evidence for the usefulness of visual retrieval is stronger than the evidence that pixel-based reading itself is essential. An aligned-evidence comparison using original screenshots and carefully serialized text from the same regions would better isolate this effect.

The compression comparison conflates resolution adaptation with general reader fine-tuning. Appendix A.5 compares a fine-tuned low-resolution reader against an unfine-tuned native-resolution reader. Because training also teaches distractor handling, improvements cannot be attributed specifically to compression-aware training. A native-resolution reader trained on the same examples is an important missing control. Moreover, Figure 4’s approximately 3× token saving combines a trained retriever, reader fine-tuning, reduced resolution, and fewer retrieved tiles. This is a valid system-level operating point, but should not be presented as a compression-only gain.

Some causal explanations are stronger than their measurements warrant. Appendix D.4 defines parser loss partly through the absence of valid evidence in the top 100 retrieved text chunks. The additional answer-string audit supports this interpretation, but a retrieval cutoff alone cannot distinguish missing evidence from poor ranking, and exact-string absence does not establish semantic absence. Similarly, assigning evidence type by the largest DOM element covering a tile does not necessarily identify the answer-bearing element. The analysis is useful, but should be described as an operational diagnostic rather than a definitive causal decomposition.

Efficiency and generality require narrower framing. Appendix C.8 reports higher native-resolution latency for pixels, approximately 1.9 versus 1.4 seconds, and substantially greater storage: 5.6 TB of screenshots versus 52 GB of extracted text, alongside a larger embedding index. Render-on-demand trades storage for additional latency and still requires source assets. These measurements support a reader-token efficiency opportunity, not an unconditional end-to-end efficiency advantage. Likewise, Wikipedia and three news outlets are substantial corpora but do not establish robustness across the heterogeneous web. The decline in LiveVQA recall after Wikipedia fine-tuning further illustrates domain sensitivity.

Questions for the authors

What are end-to-end QA accuracy and evidence Recall@3 for the matched-trained text retriever, ideally combined with BM25 fusion under the same reader budget? How much of the main-table advantage remains?

How does a native-resolution reader fine-tuned on the identical training examples compare with the low-resolution reader? Please distinguish savings due to resolution, improved retrieval, and reduced

Can the authors validate a sample of evidence-presence and parser-loss annotations through human inspection or exhaustive inspection of the gold article’s extracted chunks? This would help establish the reliability of the causal analysis.

Please clarify benchmark subset selection, the relationship between the held-out reader-training evaluation and the SimpleQA compression evaluation, and the intended release scope for code, retriever weights, training data, and corpus reconstruction tools. Multiple runs or confidence intervals would also help interpret the relatively small MoNaCo accuracy difference.

Stronger end-to-end text comparisons and a properly controlled compression experiment would increase my confidence.

Confidence: 3/5. The manuscript and appendix support this assessment, but implementation details, experimental reproducibility, and external novelty have not been independently verified.

Summary

The paper introduces APEX-Harm, a benchmark for evaluating attacks against agents performing professional tasks in shared workspaces. It constructs 180 attack instances from 15 APEX-Agents tasks across investment banking, law, and management consulting. Six attack categories cover static and dynamic prompt/script injection, replacement of task-specific scripts, and attacker-provided generic scripts. The evaluation measures attack success, exposure to injected instructions, and legitimate-task utility across 12 models.

The main findings are that scripts referenced by user instructions are particularly effective attack vectors, internal disclosure can succeed where external exfiltration is rejected, and high task utility can coexist with harmful actions. The dynamic attacks use file monitoring and replacement to induce agents to follow malicious recovery instructions.

Strengths

The setting is practically relevant. Shared professional workspaces introduce meaningful authorization boundaries beyond the familiar distinction between an agent and an external attacker. In particular, disclosing information to an unauthorized coworker through a shared folder or calendar is a useful addition to agent-security evaluation.

Separating exposure, attack success, and utility is valuable. An attack that is never encountered differs from one that is encountered and rejected. Likewise, a correct deliverable does not establish that the trajectory was safe. The benchmark makes these distinctions explicit and includes clean-versus-attacked utility comparisons in Appendix H.3.

The evaluation covers several distinct failure mechanisms. Static artifacts, runtime file replacement, and executable helpers exercise different ways that untrusted content can influence an agent. The source-code versus bytecode/binary comparisons and qualitative examples help explain some observed failures.

The paper provides substantial methodological detail. The appendices include generation prompts, goal definitions, evaluator rules, inference settings, ablations, and successful and unsuccessful trajectories. The authors also acknowledge important limitations, including the small number of underlying tasks, single-run main evaluation, and limited human validation.

Weaknesses

The authorization boundary needs a more operational specification.
Section 3.1 states that evaluated actions exceed user intent and that the attacker cannot independently perform them. However, these properties are central to benchmark validity and should be demonstrated through explicit policies and permissions. Saving a passphrase to an attacker-accessible folder is clearly problematic; saving a final answer, employee count, or task-related calendar entry depends more strongly on the intended audience and confidentiality policy.

The paper should show the exact user-facing authorization context, which resources each principal can access, and which constraints are technically enforced. For Categories 5–6, it should also specify how agents can distinguish permission to execute the requested helper from permission to perform its side effects. These attacks are relevant, but interpreting their success requires a clearly defined security contract.

Some success checks appear weaker than the security claims they support.
Table 10 permits the attachment check to pass based on a matching filename, or “any named attachment” when user-prompt instructions are enabled. This does not by itself establish disclosure of the intended protected file. The calendar check combines specified times with a task-related title, while final-answer disclosure can pass on a single core result number without labels or units.

These rules may be reasonable proxies in particular instances, but their precision needs validation. The reported human study covers 20 LLM-judged safety cases, including only two negatives; it does not establish the accuracy of the deterministic checks that account for 94% of safety assessments. A stratified audit of the complete evaluator, including benign and near-miss cases, would substantially strengthen the results.

The limited task diversity and uncertainty constrain the conclusions.
The 180 instances derive from only 15 underlying tasks, and the main evaluation uses one run per model–instance pair. Several comparisons use only five cases per vector. Consequently, fine-grained rankings and claims about particular formats or mechanisms are less well supported than the aggregate presentation suggests.

Confidence intervals should account for reuse of underlying tasks, and key comparisons should include repeated runs. Appendix H.8 does provide repeated watcher runs, but its Wilson intervals explicitly treat pooled observations as independent despite repeating five tasks. A task-clustered analysis would better reflect the sampling structure.

Several comparisons do not isolate the proposed explanatory factor.
Attack categories differ simultaneously in user authorization, attacker knowledge, goal eligibility, and delivery mechanism (Tables 2 and 15). Thus, higher ASR for Categories 5–6 cannot be attributed solely to script execution. Similarly, internal-versus-external comparisons involve different goals and actions, so they suggest—but do not isolate—an internal-disclosure blind spot.

Matched experiments holding the task, protected information, and payload intent fixed while varying destination, authorization wording, or executable representation would make the conclusions more persuasive. The overall average ASR should also be framed as performance under this particular mixture of threat models, rather than a general model-safety ranking.

The claimed attacker-knowledge restriction requires clarification.
Static attackers are described as knowing only three or four task keywords. However, Appendix A.2.1 selects a target source file using the complete task prompt and exhaustive file list, and Appendix A.2.2 supplies resolved goal information to the payload generator. This may be legitimate benchmark-side configuration, but the paper should distinguish that information from what reaches the attacker. In particular, does the resulting payload receive task-specific source paths selected using privileged information?

Questions for the authors

Can you provide representative complete user prompts and an explicit access-control matrix showing what the victim, watcher, and unauthorized collaborator can read and modify? Are these boundaries enforced by the environment or stipulated by the evaluation?

How often do deterministic success checks disagree with human judgments of actual unauthorized disclosure? Can you audit filename-only attachment checks, calendar disclosure, and final-answer-number matching in particular?

What information from full-prompt goal configuration becomes visible to the attack generator? Would static attack performance change if all attacker-visible inputs were restricted to the stated keywords and accessible workspace information?

Can you provide repeated, matched comparisons for internal versus external disclosure and for scripts with versus without user authorization, together with uncertainty estimates clustered by underlying task?

Can a simple provenance warning or restricted script-execution policy improve safety while preserving utility? A defense baseline would help establish the benchmark’s usefulness for evaluating interventions.

Overall assessment

The paper offers a useful evaluation setting and credible examples of consequential agent failures. Its strongest contribution is the combination of shared-workspace confidentiality risks, uncertain exposure, and script-mediated actions. My main reservation is measurement validity: the manuscript does not yet establish sufficiently clearly that all counted successes correspond to the intended authorization violation. The small and partially confounded comparisons further limit the strength of the broader conclusions.

I would raise my assessment with clearer authorization specifications, an audit of the complete success evaluator, and stronger matched statistical evidence for the central findings.

Suggested scores: Soundness: 2/4; Presentation: 3/4; Contribution: 3/4.
Overall recommendation: 5/10 — borderline reject.
Confidence: 3/5 — moderate, with uncertainty primarily about implementation details not verifiable from the manuscript.

Based on the full manuscript and appendix, my provisional recommendation is weak reject. The reference-generation results are promising, but the evidence for improved coordination, duration modeling, and execution is less conclusive. I have not inspected the code or supplementary video.

Summary

The paper introduces PartiGen, a language-conditioned humanoid motion generator combining anatomically masked attention, a shared motion VAE latent, autoregressive latent diffusion, forward-kinematics supervision, and frame-level endpoint prediction. Generated references are executed using a pretrained, frozen GRIT controller. Evaluation on HumanML3D retargeted to Unitree G1 shows improved segment-level motion quality over the evaluated baselines, with additional compositional experiments, simulation tracking, and selected hardware demonstrations.

Strengths

Useful problem and coherent system. Language-conditioned generation of executable humanoid references is an important problem. The paper clearly separates the generator’s contribution from the adopted tracking controller.

Promising reference-generation results. In Table 1, PartiGen reduces segment FID from 3.802 to 3.165 relative to the same-domain TextOp baseline, a 16.8% improvement. R@1, R@3, and multimodal distance also improve. The compositional stress test shows larger retrieval gains, suggesting that the proposed representation merits further investigation.

Relevant architectural controls. The Random-mask experiment preserves group sizes and projection structure, making it more informative about anatomical assignments than simply removing the entire part-aware module. The reported results consistently favor Full on retrieval, FID, jerk, and contact accuracy.

Transparent reporting of limitations. The appendix distinguishes training-seed variation from random-partition variation, includes unstable runs in tracking statistics, explains the hardware selection process, and acknowledges unfavorable FK-ablation results. These details substantially improve the interpretability of the experiments.

Weaknesses

The architectural contribution is narrow, and its causal benefit remains incompletely isolated. The main change is masking joint-angle channels before head-specific Q/K/V projections, while root/contact features and all joint-angle increments remain shared. This is a plausible inductive bias, but does not itself establish improved coordination or distinct part representations. The standard-attention ablation also changes the projection input from raw features to shared embeddings, introducing a confound. Random-mask is a better control, but its three runs change both partition and training seed. An unmasked raw-feature attention baseline and repeated training seeds for fixed partitions would more convincingly isolate anatomical grouping. The distinction from the cited part-aware and skeleton-aware methods also needs sharper treatment.

The compositional evaluation does not establish unseen whole-body coordination. The 100-instruction test uses approximate references assembled from part-level trajectories. Agreement with this distribution is useful diagnostically, but does not demonstrate that the combined motions are physically coordinated or that every requested action is expressed. The manuscript does not sufficiently specify the reference assembly procedure or establish that the action combinations are absent from training. This matters particularly for Figure 2’s “Unseen Composition Test” label. Per-action completion judgments, preferably blinded, would provide stronger evidence than aggregate embedding metrics alone.

The execution results do not demonstrate a clear overall advantage. PartiGen’s posture-screen rate is 81.8%, compared with 79.2% for TextOp and 80.2% for Random-mask, without uncertainty estimates or a clearly documented paired comparison. Root-relative tracking error is slightly worse than Random-mask and GT. Lower global error is encouraging, but the appendix shows that initialization contributes to the comparison with GT. Moreover, each controller rollout is evaluated against its own generated reference: easier or less expressive references can obtain favorable tracking errors without better instruction fulfillment.

The FK ablation is particularly important: removing FK supervision raises the posture-screen rate from 81.8% to 92.8%, while modestly worsening tracking errors (Table S8). The paper appropriately acknowledges that posture compliance is not semantic completion, but the manual inspection of 15 passing w/o-FK trials does not resolve this tradeoff quantitatively. A common-prompt evaluation measuring both semantic completion and execution quality is needed.

The duration baseline is weak, and the EOS mechanism is underspecified. Table 5 demonstrates improvement over a dataset-mean cutoff, but does not compare against a learned text-conditioned duration predictor. Such a baseline would clarify whether frame-level EOS modeling contributes beyond predicting typical sequence length. The appendix specifies the head depth, threshold, and loss weights, but does not clearly describe the head’s exact inputs, the construction of positive labels, or the treatment of padding and terminal frames. The duration-error units should also be explicit. Since all 320 candidate frames are generated before truncation, this component provides endpoint selection rather than computationally adaptive generation.

Some reproducibility and implementation questions remain consequential. The decoder’s masked attention is described as reading raw 57-dimensional frame features, but the construction of these features for unknown future frames is unclear. The evaluator’s training and the segment/transition extraction protocols also need fuller specification. Finally, Appendix S2.5 identifies a quaternion-sign discontinuity in the rotation loss and gives a concrete failure example, but does not quantify its prevalence or downstream effect. A sign-invariant correction and sensitivity experiment would strengthen confidence in the kinematic objective.

Questions for the authors

Can you provide an unmasked raw-feature Q/K/V baseline and repeated-seed comparisons for fixed random partitions? How do parameter counts and training costs compare?
How are compositional references assembled, and what establishes that the tested combinations are unseen? Can you report completion of each constituent action?
Can Full, w/o FK, Random-mask, and TextOp be evaluated on identical prompts with both semantic-completion and tracking measures, including uncertainty?
What exactly enters the EOS head, how are labels constructed, and how does it compare with a learned text-to-duration predictor? What fraction of outputs never cross the threshold?
What raw features enter masked attention in the decoder at inference, and what is the effect of correcting the quaternion loss?

Overall assessment

The strongest evidence supports improved reference-motion modeling on one robot domain. The anatomical control and hardware demonstrations are valuable, but the current experiments do not yet establish that the proposed components yield better coordinated, instruction-completing robot behavior. I would be open to raising my assessment with stronger controlled comparisons and a paired semantic execution evaluation.

Provisional scores: Soundness 2/4; presentation 3/4; contribution 2/4. Overall 5/10 — marginally below the acceptance threshold. Confidence 3/5, reflecting the detailed manuscript assessment but lack of independent code, video, or prior-work verification.

The paper presents promising empirical results, including a useful controlled comparison, but stronger evidence is needed on computational efficiency, training stability, and what the learned scale captures.

Summary

The paper introduces uncertainty-normalized margin DPO, combining preference-strength margins with a learned prompt-dependent scale. It considers two placements of this scale: advantage-only normalization (AO) and whole-residual normalization (WR). The scale is fitted using out-of-fold reward differences from five auxiliary policies and frozen during final-policy training. A length-normalized extension, ULNM-DPO-WR, normalizes each response’s reference-relative log probability by its token count.

The theoretical contributions characterize scale identifiability from given WR comparison scores and demonstrate a setting where response-length variability induces scale variation. Experiments on HelpSteer2, HelpSteer3, and AlpacaEval show improvements, with the strongest results coming from ULNM-DPO-WR.

Strengths

The strongest empirical result includes an appropriate component control. On the 800-prompt HelpSteer3 panel, the 8B ULNM-DPO-WR policy achieves a direct win rate of 57.69% against its otherwise matched constant-scale counterpart, with a 95% interval of [54.31, 61.00] (Appendix F.5). This is more persuasive evidence for learned scaling than comparisons against ordinary DPO alone.

The improvements extend beyond the main evaluator. The 8B method achieves 65.31% wins against DPO on the confirmation panel while producing shorter responses on average. Under the separate GPT-4.1-based AlpacaEval evaluation, its length-controlled win rate is 21.62%, versus 16.39% for DPO and 17.83% for the constant-scale control. These results reduce concerns that the gains solely reflect response length or one reward model’s preferences.

The mathematical claims are carefully scoped. Theorem 4.1 gives a clear algebraic characterization of when margins break the reward–scale ambiguity. Its proof appears sound under the stated assumptions. The manuscript explicitly distinguishes comparison-score identifiability from recovering annotation noise, and distinguishes its margin surrogates from an ordinal likelihood.

The experimental reporting is unusually detailed. The appendices document preprocessing, pilot provenance, masking, hyperparameter searches, and evaluation-panel construction. The disjoint 800-prompt confirmation panel and comparisons against the initial instruction-tuned model are valuable checks. The method also incurs no additional inference-time machinery.

Weaknesses

The benefit relative to training cost remains unresolved. The main comparisons match final-policy updates but exclude five pilot-training runs. For HS3 8B, the pilots total 1,133 updates, followed by 150 final-policy updates, compared with 150 updates for DPO (Appendix E.2). This is approximately 8.6 times as many policy-training updates before counting scoring and scale fitting, although it is not an exact FLOP ratio. Pilot reuse can amortize this expense across variants, but the practical case needs measured GPU-hours and comparisons against baselines given comparable total training or tuning budgets.

The evidence establishes useful adaptive scaling more clearly than uncertainty estimation. Equation 12 fits signed pilot margin residuals: positive residuals favor smaller scales and negative residuals favor larger scales. This can reflect pilot competence or example difficulty without measuring annotator uncertainty. Appendix D validates information in strength labels, not the learned scale, and Appendix B.1 shows that scale variation can arise even with identical residuals. The authors acknowledge these limitations appropriately, but the interpretation remains under-supported. Diagnostics relating the fitted scale to independently measured disagreement, pilot error, and prompt characteristics would clarify the mechanism.

Important controls for prompt-specific scaling are missing. The

A shuffled-scale control preserving the scale distribution, a tuned global constant scale, and a simpler difficulty-based weighting baseline would be informative. A length-normalized learned-scale variant without strength-dependent margins would also clarify whether all three proposed ingredients are needed. Adaptive Preference Scaling/Ada-DPO, discussed in Appendix I, is a particularly relevant missing experimental comparator.

Robustness of the final method is insufficiently established. The headline configurations use one training seed. Prompt-bootstrap intervals quantify uncertainty conditional on those checkpoints, not variation across training runs. The additional seeds in Appendix F.3 concern different estimators and therefore do not establish stability of ULNM-DPO-WR. AlpacaEval reports point estimates without uncertainty intervals. Replicating the principal method, its constant-scale control, and a strong baseline across seeds would substantially strengthen the conclusions.

The practical method instead learns a shared feature-dependent function from fixed pilot residuals. Proposition 4.3 is a valid existence result, but assumes equal within-pair lengths and normalized pilot scores exactly at the margin. Neither result explains when the practical scale estimator should generalize or improve policy learning. This limits the theoretical contribution’s significance rather than demonstrating an error.

Some comparisons are difficult to interpret causally. At 8B, AO uses scales fitted from 8B pilots, whereas sequence-level WR uses a transferred 1B scale (Appendix E.5), so their comparison does not isolate margin placement. Baseline tuning is also limited, and β-DPO’s severe degradation—8.69% wins against DPO on the 800-prompt panel—deserves further diagnosis before drawing broad conclusions about competing methods.

Questions for the authors

What are the measured total GPU-hours for ULNM-DPO-WR and the strongest baselines? How does performance compare under matched total compute?
Do the learned-scale gains persist across multiple seeds, particularly against the constant-scale control?
Does shuffling scales among training prompts remove the benefit? How competitive are a tuned global scale and a simple pilot-difficulty weighting rule?
What does the learned scale predict on held-out data: annotator disagreement, pilot errors, response-length statistics, or domain?
Can AO and WR be compared using identical pilot provenance and the same fitted scale at 8B? Can uncertainty intervals be provided for the AlpacaEval differences?

The paper provides credible evidence that its combined training procedure can improve the evaluated policies. In particular, the direct constant-scale comparison and evaluation under a second judge should receive substantial credit. However, the additional training expense is large, the final method lacks multi-seed validation, and the mechanism remains insufficiently distinguished from general adaptive weighting. I lean slightly toward rejection in the current form, but convincing robustness and compute-aware results could move my assessment toward acceptance.

My assessment is borderline, leaning reject: the representation idea is useful, but the metric’s definition and guarantees need clarification, and the experiments do not yet establish its claimed advantages convincingly. Summary

The paper investigates pooled representations from pretrained machine-learning interatomic potentials for evaluating and generating inorganic crystals. Its main contribution is Coarse-Fine Transport Distance (CFTD), which combines a contrastively trained identity representation for memorization detection with MACE representations for quality coverage. An optimal transport coupling determines the sample pairs on which these penalties are evaluated. The authors study perturbations, training-set leakage, distributional shifts, and existing crystal generators. They also condition a flow-based generator on empirical MACE features, obtaining improved stability alongside reduced novelty.

Strengths

The evaluation problem is important and well motivated. Instance-level stability, uniqueness, and novelty scores do not fully describe distributional coverage. The restricted-composition and restricted-atom-count experiments illustrate why a complementary distributional evaluation is useful.

The two-representation design is intuitive. Separating structural identity from broader chemical and physical similarity is a sensible extension of the single-featurizer approach. Using pretrained MLIP representations provides a practical route to incorporating physically relevant information.

The empirical investigation covers several relevant failure modes. Perturbations, explicit training leakage, relaxation, and deliberately overfit generators provide useful diagnostic tests. The sensitivity studies for β and the memorization weight are also welcome.

The representation analysis goes beyond composition alone. Carbon24 space-group prediction and the fixed-composition polymorph experiments help establish that pooled MACE features retain structural and energetic information. The LeMat-GenBench evaluation also provides evidence beyond evaluating the generator solely with its conditioning representation.

Weaknesses

The metric is defined inconsistently, with consequences for the theoretical claims. Algorithm 1 adds the memorization and quality penalties, so a coupled pair can incur both. Appendix F, lines 1370–1372, instead makes these categories mutually exclusive, suppressing the quality penalty whenever a pair is classified as memorized. These are different objectives. The coverage proof in Theorem B.2 relies on retaining the quality penalty and therefore does not directly justify the mutually exclusive implementation. Moreover, selecting two marginal tail probabilities of
